# A general-body bridge for the joint-row inequalities at a symmetry center

This is a scoped ordinary theorem. The body need not be a simplex or
polytope, but it must be centrally symmetric and the source must be its
symmetry center. No asymmetric or mixed-fiber conclusion is asserted.

## 1. The actual cap/section vector

Let d>=2, K=-K be a convex body in R^d, and let nonzero normals
v_1,...,v_(d+1) span R^d and sum to zero. Define

    q_i=|K intersect {v_i.x>=0}|/|K|=1/2,
    sigma_i=H_(d-1)(K intersect v_i^perp)/||v_i||,
    p_i=(1/sigma_i)/sum_j(1/sigma_j),
    f_i=d [(q_i/sigma_i)/sum_j(q_j/sigma_j)]/q_i^(1/d)
       =d 2^(1/d) p_i.                                  (1)

Every sigma_i is finite and positive because zero is interior to K.
This is exactly the extension of the simplex f-vector defined using
the actual cap volumes and coarea section measures.

We use the standard Busemann theorem: the intersection body of an
origin-symmetric convex body is convex. Its radial function at a unit
vector u is H_(d-1)(K intersect u^perp). Thus its gauge is

    N(v)=||v||/H_(d-1)(K intersect v^perp)=1/sigma(v),

which is a norm. The precise symmetry hypothesis is essential. A
primary mathematical source recording this classical statement is
Kim--Yaskin--Zvavitch, *The geometry of p-convex intersection bodies*,
[arXiv:1006.1546](https://arxiv.org/abs/1006.1546). Only this ordinary
named theorem is imported; the finite-vector consequences below are
proved directly.

By norm subadditivity and v_i=-sum_(j!=i)v_j,

    N(v_i)<=sum_(j!=i)N(v_j),

so p_i<=1/2 for every i.

## 2. A proved finite-mixture reduction and the joint inequalities

The polytope

    P={p: p_i>=0, sum p_i=1, p_i<=1/2}

is the convex hull of the vectors (e_j+e_k)/2, j!=k. Here is an
elementary proof. If a point is not one of those vectors, it has at
least two coordinates strictly between zero and one half: exactly one
such coordinate is incompatible with sum p=1 and the other coordinates
being zero or one half. Perturb two fractional coordinates in opposite
directions until one reaches an endpoint. The original point is a
convex combination of the two resulting endpoints. Repeating on the
finite number of fractional coordinates proves the claim.

Consequently the actual vector f in (1) is a convex combination of

    z^(jk)=(d 2^(1/d)/2)(e_j+e_k).                      (2)

For a fixed selected i the function

    Phi_i(f)=f_i+(d-1)[(sum_(j!=i)f_j)/d]^(d/(d-1))

is convex and continuous on the nonnegative orthant. On a vector (2),
its value is exactly

    Phi_in=d 2^(-(d-1)/d)+(d-1)/2,       if i is in {j,k},
    Phi_out=(d-1)2^(1/(d-1)),           otherwise.       (3)

Both are at most d. Indeed (1+1/r)^r>=2 for every integer r>=1:
the first two binomial terms already sum to two. Applying this with
r=d-1 gives Phi_out<=d, and applying it with r=d gives
d 2^(1/d)<=d+1, or Phi_in<=d. Thus Jensen's inequality proves

    f_i+(d-1)[(sum_(j!=i)f_j)/d]^(d/(d-1))<=d             (4)

for every actual centrally symmetric body at its symmetry center.

In fact the inequality is strict. For d>=3, both comparisons in (3)
are strict. For d=2 only Phi_out can equal d. In any pair mixture
representing p, the total mass of pairs containing i is 2p_i>0, and
Phi_in<d. Jensen therefore remains strict.

More precisely, the mixture argument retains the exact bound

    Phi_i(f)<=2p_i Phi_in+(1-2p_i)Phi_out.                (5)

For d=2 it gives the explicit positive deficit

    2-Phi_i(f)>=p_i(3-2sqrt(2))>0.

## 3. Relation to actual simplex row data

The vectors (2) are limits of actual positive simplex row data. This
statement concerns cap/section data, not a decomposition of K itself.
Fix a pair {j,k}. Start with the balanced symmetric matrix having

    a_j=a_k=b_jk=b_kj=1/2

and all other entries zero. For 0<epsilon<1, mix this data with the
strictly positive balanced data

    a_i=1/(d+1),       b_il=1/[d(d+1)] for i!=l.

Let M_epsilon have diagonal a_i and off-diagonal -b_il. It is symmetric,
has column sums zero, and is positive definite on the sum-zero subspace.
Indeed its uniform component is

    (1/d)I-[1/(d(d+1))]11^T,

positive definite there, while its pair component is positive
semidefinite. Hence M_epsilon has rank d and kernel span{1}.

Take its first d rows as coordinates of d+1 points P_i in R^d. These
are affinely independent: a dependence with coefficient sum zero lies
in ker M_epsilon and is therefore zero. Their centroid is zero because
the row sums vanish. For the canonical normals e_1,...,e_d,-sum e_j,
their full evaluation matrix is M_epsilon. Thus all cuts isolate one
strict vertex and the source is interior to an actual simplex.

Formula (2) of the simplex joint-row theorem gives, as epsilon decreases
to zero,

    f_j,f_k -> d[1*(1/2)^(d-1)]^(1/d)=d2^(1/d)/2,
    f_i ->0 for all other i.

Therefore f lies in the closed convex hull of actual simplex f-vectors.
This is one precise mixture bridge using actual section geometry.
It does not claim a mixture of convex bodies, preservation of each q_i
under the limiting simplex construction, or compatibility with other
integer fibers. General asymmetric bodies and noncentral sources are
not covered by Busemann's theorem used here.
